title: Never alone
hook: when you shut the door and darken the room, you're not alone: God is within, and your own spirit (Discourses 1.14)

segments.voice: Yesterday: brothers by nature, the servant as kin. Were you gentle with someone who served you? Day four hundred. Four hundred days on the hill.

Late at night, door shut, lights off, phone face down. Nobody can see you. This is the hour when people eat the thing they swore off, send the message they'll regret, or lie awake feeling more alone than they've felt all day. It feels like the one hour that doesn't count, because no one is watching. Epictetus told his students that hour is an illusion. The room is never as empty as it looks. Today: never alone.
screen: `DOOR SHUT, LIGHTS OFF.` → `THE HOUR THAT DOESN'T COUNT.` → `THE ROOM ISN'T EMPTY.`

segments.voice: This is Discourses book one, chapter fourteen. A student asks: can a person really believe God sees everything they do? Epictetus answers with the whole world. Don't you see, he says, that everything is bound together? Plants bloom and bear fruit in their season, as if at a signal. Living things change with the moon and the sun. If plants and our bodies are that closely linked to the whole, how much more our minds, which for the Stoics are pieces of the same reason that runs it all. Then comes the image. God, he says, has set beside each person a guardian spirit, a daimon, who never sleeps and can't be fooled. So when you've shut your doors and made it dark inside, remember never to say you're alone. You're not. God is within, and your own spirit is within, and they need no light to see what you're doing. For the Stoics, this God isn't someone peering in from outside. It's the reason in you, which is never off duty. The same chapter compares it to a soldier's oath: soldiers swear loyalty to the emperor, Epictetus says, and we should swear an oath too, to honor what's within us. Other traditions say something nearby in their own way. A psalm in the King James words says, "If I say, Surely the darkness shall cover me; even the night shall be light about me." The two aren't the same teaching, and each is held on its own terms. But both refuse to let the dark room be a place that doesn't count.
screen: `EVERYTHING IS BOUND TOGETHER.` · `A GUARDIAN WHO NEVER SLEEPS.` · `DOORS SHUT, YOU'RE NOT ALONE.` · `A SOLDIER'S OATH.` · then, large: `NEVER ALONE.`

segments.voice: If you can, find a quiet room and close the door. Dim the light if you like. Sit, and let the breath slow. Notice the feeling of being unseen. Then, in whatever way fits what you believe, notice that you're still here with yourself: the part of you that watches, that knows what you're doing, that never quite switches off. Sit with that company for a while. Nothing to hide from it, nothing to perform for it. The bell holds the time.
Never alone. Epictetus' reminder for the dark room: God is within, and your own guardian spirit, and neither needs light to see.
Your line: never alone. Tonight, when the door is shut and no one can see, act the way you would if the room were full. Day four hundred.

howItsDone: Many people who read Epictetus use this chapter as a nighttime reminder, treating the private, unseen hours as just as real as the public ones.

original.note: Greek daimōn: a guardian spirit; Epictetus says God set one beside each person, and Socrates spoke of his own inner sign (daimonion).

trapdoor: what you thought: someone's always watching you.
what it means: you carry your own witness, the reason within, wherever you go.
what a scholar hears: Stoic daimon is close to the inner rational self; Marcus Aurelius uses the same word for the guiding reason within each person.
